name: Austrian Wiener Schnitzel
description: Wiener schnitzel is a protected term in Austria requiring real veal, which chicken breast stands in for here as a widely available substitute; real technique uses plain breadcrumbs, not panko, and a genuine 'souffleing' motion - gently shaking the pan while frying so the breading puffs and separates slightly from the meat. Real Viennese tradition serves it simply with lemon and no sauce at all - red cabbage and spätzle are German additions, not Austrian ones.

ingredients_full.note: pounded thin, standing in for veal

ingredients.note: pounded thin, standing in for veal

steps_detailed: Season the pounded chicken with a pinch of salt.
Dredge in the flour, then the beaten egg, then the breadcrumbs, coating evenly at each stage.
Heat the butter and oil together in a pan until foaming.

Fry the cutlet, gently shaking the pan back and forth as it cooks, 2-3 minutes per side, until deeply golden - this real 'souffleing' motion is what makes the breading puff slightly away from the meat.
Serve immediately with a lemon wedge and nothing else - real Viennese tradition skips sauce, red cabbage, and spätzle entirely.

name: Austrian Kaiserschmarrn
description: Kaiserschmarrn, a torn, shredded pancake named for Emperor Franz Joseph I, depends on a real soufflé-style technique - the egg whites are whipped separately to stiff peaks and folded into the batter, which is what gives it its real light, fluffy texture, not a technique to skip for convenience.
steps_detailed: Whisk the egg yolks with the milk, flour, and half the sugar into a smooth batter.
In a separate, clean bowl, beat the egg whites with the remaining sugar until stiff peaks form.
Gently fold the whipped whites into the batter in two additions, keeping as much air in as possible - real technique depends on this real fold, not a full mix.
Melt the butter in an oven-safe pan, pour in the batter, and scatter the raisins over the top.
Cook over medium heat 2-3 minutes until the bottom sets, then transfer to a 400F (200C) oven for 8-10 minutes until puffed and golden.
Tear into rough pieces directly in the pan and dust with powdered sugar before serving.

name: Austrian Käsespätzle
description: Käsespätzle, soft egg noodles baked with real melted cheese and caramelized onion, is Austria's real answer to mac and cheese, especially beloved in the alpine regions.
steps_detailed: Cook the pasta per package directions.
Cook the onion in the butter over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, 15-18 minutes, until deeply caramelized.
Toss the cooked pasta with the cheese while still hot so it melts, then top with the caramelized onion.

name: Austrian Goulash (Wiener Saftgulasch)
description: Wiener saftgulasch, a real Viennese-style beef goulash, is genuinely built on a mountain of onions - real technique uses roughly as much onion by weight as meat, cooked down until they melt into the sauce.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion in a little oil over medium heat, stirring occasionally, 20-25 minutes, until deeply softened and reduced - real technique depends on this large volume of onion melting down.
Add the garlic and paprika, and cook 1 minute.
Add the beef, tomato paste, broth, and vinegar, and simmer 45-50 minutes until the beef is fall-apart tender.

name: Austrian Apfelstrudel
description: Apfelstrudel, apples wrapped in real paper-thin pastry, is a genuine Austrian icon, real technique tossing the apples with breadcrumbs first to absorb their juices so the pastry stays crisp.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Apples, raw, gala, with skin (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)

ingredients.ingredient: Apples, raw, gala, with skin (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)

steps_detailed: Toss the apples with the breadcrumbs, sugar, cinnamon, and raisins - real technique lets the breadcrumbs soak up the apples' juices so the pastry doesn't turn soggy.
Layer the phyllo sheets, brushing each with melted butter.
Spread the apple mixture along one edge and roll up tightly.
Bake at 375F (190C) for 30-35 minutes until deeply golden.

name: Austrian Tafelspitz
description: Tafelspitz, boiled beef served with real horseradish and apple sauce, was reportedly Emperor Franz Joseph's favorite dish, real technique simmering the beef low and slow with root vegetables for a genuinely rich broth.
steps_detailed: Simmer the beef with the carrot, onion, and bay leaf in enough water to cover, 1.5-2 hours, until genuinely fork-tender.
Slice the beef and serve with the horseradish alongside.

name: Austrian Erdäpfelsalat (Potato Salad)
description: Erdäpfelsalat, a real vinegar-and-broth-dressed potato salad without mayonnaise, is the traditional Austrian side for schnitzel, real technique dressing the potatoes while still warm so they absorb the tangy dressing.
steps_detailed: Boil the potatoes until tender, 15-18 minutes, then slice while still warm.
Whisk the onion, vinegar, broth, and oil together.
Toss the warm potato slices with the dressing right away, so they absorb it fully.

name: Austrian Sachertorte
description: Sachertorte, a dense chocolate cake with real apricot jam and chocolate glaze, is one of Vienna's most famous exports, real technique spreading a thin layer of apricot jam between the cake and glaze.
steps_detailed: Cream the butter and sugar, then mix in the egg, flour, and cocoa into a smooth batter.
Bake at 350F (175C) for 20-22 minutes until set.
Once cooled, spread a thin layer of apricot jam over the top before serving.
